scenes.heading: Repartition
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Repartition and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: What repartition does
items: Changes the number of partitions in a DataFrame
Triggers a full shuffle to redistribute rows
Can partition by column(s) for even spread
scenes.narration: Repartition reshapes how your data is divided across the cluster by setting a new partition count. Because it must move rows between executors to balance them, it always performs a full shuffle. You can also repartition by a column so that rows sharing a key land together.

scenes.heading: repartition vs coalesce
scenes.narration: Repartition and coalesce both change partition counts but differ sharply in cost. Repartition reshuffles all data and can both grow and shrink the count while producing evenly sized partitions. Coalesce merges existing partitions without a full shuffle, so it is cheaper but can only reduce the count and may leave uneven sizes.

scenes.code:
df = spark.read.parquet("/data/events")  # 4 large partitions
# Increase parallelism before a heavy transform
wide = df.repartition(200)
# Or co-locate rows by key to prepare a join
by_key = df.repartition(200, "user_id")
by_key.groupBy("user_id").count().show()
scenes.heading: Two common patterns
scenes.narration: The first repartition raises the partition count to two hundred to increase parallelism ahead of a compute-heavy transformation. The second repartitions by user_id, which uses hash partitioning so all rows for a user land in the same partition. That key-based layout can make a subsequent groupBy or join cheaper because matching keys are already co-located. Both forms pay a shuffle cost up front.

scenes.text: Repartition is a wide transformation; use it deliberately, not by habit.
scenes.narration: Because each repartition triggers a full shuffle, adding one carelessly can cost more than the work you were trying to speed up. Reach for it when you genuinely need more parallelism or key co-location.
